completeSourceDiscovery.boundaryContinuationRule: a move beginning in lookbehind remains owned by the predecessor chunk

candidateRows: Qualia resist physical reduction because their felt first-person character is the phenomenon to be explained, not merely an external phenomenon's mental effect.
This supplies Huemer's principal argument in the chunk for treating conscious experience as nonphysical and therefore supports the substance-dualist side of the motion.

After defining qualia through the character of conscious experience, Huemer contrasts them with successful reductions such as heat and argues that reduction cannot set aside felt character when felt character is precisely what requires explanation.
Mary's acquisition of experiential knowledge is compatible with identity theory because fully knowing certain physical brain states may require occupying those states.
This is Oppy's main answer to the knowledge argument, offering a naturalistic account of why new experience need not imply a nonphysical property or substance.
Huemer's claim that the irreducible felt character of qualia cannot be captured by a physical account.

Oppy reconstructs the black-and-white-room case, identifies perceptual states largely with brain states, and argues that Mary's limitation may consist in not occupying the relevant state rather than lacking knowledge of a nonphysical fact.
The knowledge argument does not essentially concern state-dependent access; it concerns knowing every physical property while still not knowing a mental state's qualitative character.
The move isolates the modal and epistemic premise needed to resist Oppy's ability-based reply and preserve the inference from new qualitative knowledge to nonphysical facts.
Oppy's proposal that experiential knowledge may be knowledge of a physical state available only by occupying that state.

Huemer distinguishes the dualist point from the claim that experience is always required for qualitative knowledge, invokes the possibility of imaginatively grasping an unexperienced shade, and returns to the stipulated gap between complete physical knowledge and qualitative knowledge.
If some physical facts can be known only by occupying corresponding physical states, Mary's confinement explains her ignorance without implying any nonphysical fact.
This preserves Oppy's physicalist-compatible treatment of Mary by denying that exhaustive physical knowledge can simply be stipulated independently of the relevant mode of access.
Huemer's contention that Mary can know all physical properties yet remain ignorant of the qualitative fact about seeing red.

Oppy argues that Mary's failure to occupy the relevant state is itself a constraint on which physical facts she knows, so the thought experiment may not coherently grant her every physical fact while withholding the experience-dependent one.
Reality contains scale-specific properties that cannot be defined from lower-scale properties, without making the lower scale metaphysically privileged or abandoning naturalism.
The scale-independence framework supplies the metaphysical basis for Oppy's view that irreducible mental properties need not belong to a separate nonphysical substance.
Huemer's assumption that a physical fact must reduce to particle locations, arrangements, mass, charge, or other microphysical facts.

Oppy rejects reduction of every property to microphysics, describes autonomous vocabularies and properties at molecular, chemical, organismic, and cosmological scales, and treats these as equally legitimate parts of one natural reality.
Oppy's scale-independence account appears substantively equivalent to an emergence theory despite his reluctance to use that label.
The challenge tests whether Oppy's alternative genuinely explains mental properties within naturalism or merely redescribes the familiar emergence position under different terminology.
Oppy's account of autonomous higher-scale properties and his denial that the lower physical scale is metaphysically privileged.
Huemer observes that the account sounded emergent until Oppy rejected the terminology and asks whether the difference is substantive or only verbal.
An organism can possess mental properties at its proper scale even though its microphysical constituents possess neither consciousness nor proto-mental properties.
This directly explains how consciousness may belong to a natural organism without requiring conscious particles, proto-conscious matter, or an additional immaterial bearer.
Huemer's suggestion that Oppy's position is substantively an emergence theory under a different label.

Oppy allows that some emergence theories might overlap with his view, then stresses that examining an organism at different scales reveals only the properties appropriate to each scale, with mental properties absent from the microphysical inventory.
Knowing what an experience is like may consist in possessing discriminatory abilities that depend on having occupied relevant perceptual states, rather than apprehending a distinct mental substance.
The move gives Oppy's positive account of phenomenal knowledge and weakens the inference from first-person experience to ontologically distinct nonphysical properties or substances.
Huemer's use of Mary's new qualitative knowledge to argue that conscious experience includes facts beyond the physical inventory.

Oppy focuses on abilities such as visually discriminating colors, argues that Mary lacks them while confined because she has not entered the requisite states, and treats knowing what an experience is like as dependent on such state-grounded capacities.
Mary gains propositional knowledge of a determinate qualitative property, not merely a skill, because her first color experience rules out alternative ways that seeing red could have felt.
This is the key rebuttal to the ability hypothesis because it restores a new phenomenal fact whose apparent absence from prior physical knowledge supports the dualist inference.
Oppy's claim that Mary's post-release gain can be understood as acquiring perceptual and discriminatory abilities grounded in new brain states.

Huemer concedes that Mary acquires practical color-identification skills but argues that she also learns which qualitative character seeing red has, thereby excluding previously open experiential possibilities.
Direct awareness of the new sensation gives Mary a concept and knowledge of its qualitative property, which remains unexplained as a physical property.
The move completes Huemer's reply by connecting direct phenomenal awareness, concept acquisition, and modal exclusion to the claim that the relevant property is not recognizably physical.
Oppy's effort to assimilate Mary's knowledge of what red looks like to abilities and state-dependent physical knowledge.

Huemer describes Mary as becoming directly aware of a sensation, forming its qualitative concept through experience, learning that this character accompanies red perception rather than alternatives, and demanding an account of how that property could be physical.
Intentionality and qualia support property dualism, while the personal-identity problem supplies the further route to substance dualism.
The move distinguishes evidence for nonphysical properties from the additional reasoning needed to establish the nonphysical substances asserted by the motion.
After the qualia discussion, Huemer clarifies the evidential role of intentionality and explains how personal identity bears the burden of moving from property to substance dualism.
Tree rings possess no intrinsic aboutness; observers instead use them as evidence through their own representational mental states.
The reply protects the intentionality argument from an apparent physical counterexample by locating representation in a mind rather than in tree rings themselves.
The proposed counterexample that physical tree rings are about the age of a tree.
The moderator offers informational correlations in tree rings as physical instances of aboutness, and Huemer answers that any such representation is derivative from mental interpretation.
Functionalist accounts can explain intentional attitudes within identity theory, making intentionality less troublesome for physicalism than consciousness or qualia.
This is Oppy's principal response to intentionality as evidence for dualism, offering a naturalistic explanatory framework compatible with brain-state identity.
Huemer's contention that intrinsic intentionality appears metaphysically incapable of being physical.
Following Huemer's account of intrinsic aboutness, Oppy invokes the compatibility of functionalism and identity theory to reduce the force of intentionality against physicalism.
Determinism precludes free will because doing otherwise would require a different past, and agents cannot now alter facts extending back to the universe's beginning.
The argument presents libertarian freedom as a feature resistant to deterministic physical explanation and therefore as part of the cumulative case for an immaterial mind.
Huemer develops a necessary-condition example and generalizes it: if every alternative action required a past that did not occur, no agent could genuinely do otherwise.
Macroscopic indeterminacy does not yield libertarian freedom, while acting from normally acquired beliefs and desires without defeating interference supplies sufficient compatibilist freedom.
The move directly contests the free-will component of the dualist case by separating determinism from robust local regularity and denying that libertarian alternatives are needed.
Huemer's argument that an inability to change the past makes determinism incompatible with genuine free will.
Oppy allows quantum chance and its possible amplification, yet argues that deliberation remains locally robust across nearby worlds and that ordinary uncoerced action is the freedom humans need.
Higher-scale behavior is not determined in a one-way fashion by lower-scale physics, since organism-level action can explain the coordinated motion of microscopic constituents.
This scale-based account answers the objection that physicalism makes rational agency merely the product of nonrational microphysical forces, preserving organism-level explanation.
The objection that physicalist beliefs are produced only by nonrational laws, neurochemistry, and lower-level forces.
Against a challenge about rational deliberation under physicalism, Oppy distinguishes temporal determination from micro-to-macro determination and rejects both as exhaustive one-way constraints.
Emergent or downward-causal organization does not establish substance dualism because the higher-scale events remain events occurring in the brain, without an additional mental substance.
The move directly addresses the motion's ontological issue by denying that higher-scale causation entails any independently existing nonphysical bearer of mental life.
The suggestion that confirmed downward causation or emergent organization would amount to a victory for substance dualists.
After downward causation is characterized as friendly to dualism, Oppy argues that the proposed account adds no mental entity beyond organized activity in a person's brain.
Nonphysical minds need not be supernatural or magical, because they may have physical causes and arise according to regular laws.
The clarification blocks an inference from nonphysical substance to supernatural intervention, allowing substance dualism to remain compatible with lawful natural causation.
Oppy's concern that many dualists seek supernatural substances rather than merely higher-scale natural organization.
The discussion shifts from physicality to naturalness, and Huemer explains that his proposed nonphysical entities can be causally integrated with brains and governed by laws.
Thoughts are not spatially located because asking where a thought is resembles a category mistake rather than an ordinary request for an object's position.
Denying spatial location to mental states supplies another claimed disanalogy between minds and physical objects, reinforcing the case for nonphysical mentality.
Asked whether mental states have locations, Huemer appeals to the intuitive oddity of locating a thought and compares the request with spatial questions about abstract entities.
Unified consciousness creates no special problem for physicalism because selective abstraction from complicated physical processes is familiar in many nonmental systems.
The reply denies that phenomenological unity requires an indivisible mental substance by treating selective descriptions of brain activity as ordinary scientific abstraction.
The unity-of-consciousness objection that a unified experience cannot be divided among distinct portions of the brain.
Near the end of the core, Oppy responds to a unity argument by comparing attention to selected aspects of mental life with abstraction from fluid flows and other complex systems.
Given an infinite past and future, being alive now has zero probability if each person can live only once, so either reincarnation occurs or the infinite-past assumption is false.
This is Huemer's principal probabilistic argument connecting personal survival and reincarnation to the temporal structure of the universe.
After the moderator requests a short account of Huemer's reincarnation case, Huemer derives a dilemma from single lives, infinite time, and present existence.
The probability-zero reasoning appears to generalize from a person's present existence to every particular thing or event occurring now, including ordinary objects without souls.
The objection challenges whether Huemer's probability argument supports reincarnation specifically rather than an indiscriminate recurrence conclusion.
Huemer's claim that a one-life theory assigns zero probability to a person's being alive at the present time.
Oppy presses that any unique present object or occurrence faces the same temporal probability problem, although offices and other ordinary objects do not possess souls.
Qualitatively identical offices may recur, but personal identity is an objective matter that cannot be settled merely by stipulating how the word identifying a person will be used.
The distinction is necessary to prevent the reincarnation argument from collapsing into a merely verbal claim about repeated qualitative duplicates.
Oppy's objection that the same recurrence reasoning would apply to offices, tables, and other things that lack souls.
Huemer concedes repeated qualitative office configurations, treats office identity as potentially semantic, and denies that future personal identity can likewise be fixed by definition.
Contemporary cosmology makes a finite past and infinite future more plausible than an infinite past, while expansion and entropy considerations also undermine cosmic recurrence.
Huemer's reincarnation argument requires an infinite past, so evidence favoring a finite past directly attacks a necessary premise of his case.
Huemer's assumption that causal reality extends infinitely into the past and permits recurring persons and conditions.
Oppy ranks the broad temporal models, favors a finite past, and argues that failed contraction cycles and increasing entropy weaken both past infinity and recurrence.
Over infinite time, chance entropy decreases and recurrence in a bounded phase space permit initial conditions to repeat, with high-to-low entropy transitions matching low-to-high transitions.
This response defends the recurrence mechanism required by Huemer's personal-survival argument against Oppy's thermodynamic objection.
Oppy's contention that increasing entropy and the failure of cosmic contraction cycles count strongly against recurrence.
Huemer accepts ordinary entropy increase but argues that rare decreases occur and that infinite time within a limited phase space guarantees repeated conditions.
Standard projections of an eternally expanding universe imply eventual proton and black-hole decay followed only by sparse radiation, so stars, people, and recurrent conditions never return.
The projected heat-death future blocks the bounded recurrent dynamics on which Huemer's entropy reply and reincarnation argument depend.
Huemer's claim that infinite time in a limited phase space guarantees recurrence despite the usual direction of entropy change.
Oppy argues that actual cosmological expansion does not supply finite cycling: matter structures decay, expansion continues, and neither protons nor persons reappear.

A universe beginning without explanation in an extraordinarily low-entropy Big Bang state is theoretically unsatisfactory, as shown by comparison with a later-origin hypothesis that fits observations from that point onward.
The argument challenges the explanatory adequacy of the finite-past cosmology that Oppy uses to defeat Huemer's reincarnation premise.
Oppy's appeal to the physically favored finite-past cosmology as evidence against an infinite past and recurring persons.
Huemer objects that a first low-entropy state would be uncaused, then uses a hypothetical 1950 origin with apparent memories to expose the same explanatory defect.
Later-origin skeptical hypotheses are unstable because every proposed starting time is superseded by a still later and allegedly better one, preventing a consistent theory choice over time.
This objection targets the principal analogy Huemer uses to portray the ordinary finite-past account as explanatorily defective.
Huemer's proposed 1950-origin hypothesis as an evidentially adequate and more probable analogue of the Big Bang theory.
Oppy argues that 1950 is inferior to 1951 and ultimately to a present-moment origin, but those shifting hypotheses cannot serve as stable theoretical commitments.
An initial cosmic state can be explained as metaphysically necessary if possible worlds share actual history and branch only where genuine physical chances develop differently.
The necessity account supplies the explanation Huemer says a finite beginning cannot possess, thereby defending finite-past cosmology against his central complaint.
Huemer's objection that any first cosmic state begins for no reason and therefore makes finite-past theories unsatisfactory.
Oppy proposes that the initial state had to occur and motivates a branching model that admits only chance-grounded possibilities rather than unrestricted conceivability.

Mental properties are called nonphysical because they appear categorically unlike paradigmatic physical properties; merely broadening the word physical to include them changes terminology rather than ontology.
The move directly explains the conceptual basis for the pro side's nonphysical classification and distinguishes substantive disagreement from verbal relabeling.
Asked what is lost by introducing nonphysicality or broadening physicality, Huemer contrasts thought with size and mass and treats inclusive physical terminology as verbal revision.
Bottom-up physical causation cannot ground free will because blind physical causes do not respond to reasons, whereas higher-level mental causation can.
The move links nonphysical mentality to reason-responsive agency and presents mental causation as the proposed escape from both deterministic and indeterministic physical causation.
Oppy's objection that indeterministic randomness undermines Huemer's argument connecting physicalism with the absence of free will.
Asked about indeterministic randomness, Huemer distinguishes his argument from the standard consequence argument and claims that blind microphysical causes cannot make conduct responsive to reasons.
A multiscale physicalist view can avoid causal overdetermination because higher- and lower-level properties need not stand in strong determination relations.
The response protects Oppy's naturalistic account of mental causation from the claim that physical determination either excludes mental causal power or produces systematic overdetermination.
Huemer's contention that bottom-up physicalism makes reason-responsive mental causation unavailable and generates an overdetermination problem.
Oppy acknowledges the standard overdetermination worry but says his account denies sufficiently strong determination relations between physical scales, thereby avoiding that consequence.
Animals with conscious mental states possess nonphysical minds, and possible reincarnation as animals could have ethical implications for their treatment.
The move extends the soul thesis beyond humans and draws a substantive consequence from the possibility that a person could later inhabit a nonhuman animal.
Huemer attributes experiences, beliefs, and desires to at least some animals, infers that they have nonphysical minds, and considers whether animal reincarnation would affect moral treatment.
Huemer's resemblance-based account of personal identity does not readily support reincarnation as an animal because an animal would not be a qualitative duplicate of the person.
The objection tests whether Huemer's proposed criterion for survival can actually yield the cross-species reincarnation consequences that he has just entertained.
Huemer's suggestion that a human person might be reincarnated as a nonperson animal and that this possibility could bear on animal ethics.
Oppy observes that qualitative resemblance did important work in Huemer's identity account and argues that ordinary animals are insufficiently similar to a person to fit that story.
Reincarnation need not depend on eternal recurrence or duplication because unknown conditions might instead cause an enduring soul to enter another living organism.
The move broadens Huemer's account of postmortem survival beyond resemblance-based recurrence, answering a vulnerability in the proposed mechanism of reincarnation.
Oppy's objection that an animal's lack of qualitative resemblance to a person prevents it from satisfying Huemer's duplicate-based identity account.
Huemer explains the multiverse and recurrence origins of his identity argument, then says recurrence is only one possible route because a soul might enter a living thing under unknown conditions.
A soul is the single subject that bears all of a person's mental states, so there is no additional distinct entity properly called a rational soul.
The passage supplies a direct account of the entity affirmed by Huemer's dualism: one nonphysical subject unifying the person's diverse mental states.
The suggestion that Cartesian rationality establishes a specially rational kind of soul that could prevent a person from becoming a nonrational animal.
Huemer identifies the soul with the mind or subject of mental states and rejects multiplying subjects for rational thoughts, sensations, and emotions experienced by the same person.
Differences between human and animal capacities can result from different brains even if humans and animals possess the same fundamental kind of soul.
The claim explains how a nonphysical soul can remain the subject of mentality while cognitive and expressive powers vary with the organism's physical brain.
The challenge that qualitative differences between human and dog minds, especially speech capacity, require correspondingly different kinds of souls.
Huemer attributes a dog's inability to speak to its brain and evolutionary history, while allowing that the dog could in principle have the same kind of soul as a human.
Theism makes souls more likely because a personal, nonphysical God would itself be a soul and would provide precedent for human souls.
The argument places the soul hypothesis within a broader metaphysical comparison and identifies theism as background evidence favoring nonphysical persons.
Huemer says theism guarantees at least one soul if God is a nonphysical person, and that knowledge of one nonhuman soul would raise the probability that humans also have souls.
Souls did not emerge during evolution but have always existed, although inhabiting a living organism requires suitable physical conditions such as an intelligence-supporting brain.
The move directly integrates Huemer's nonphysical-substance view with biological evolution by distinguishing a soul's existence from its ability to inhabit a suitable organism.
The audience question asking at what evolutionary stage souls emerged and the follow-up concern about when a specifically human soul could enter an organism.

Huemer denies that souls originated in evolutionary history, then says embodiment requires an appropriately constituted object and speculates that suitable brains appeared only after billions of years.
A surviving disembodied soul probably cannot think or act because brain damage can impair every human capacity and death destroys the entire brain.
The claim sharply specifies what bodily death leaves intact on Huemer's view: the subject may survive, but its ordinary mental and practical capacities do not remain operative.
The follow-up question whether a disembodied soul retains rational thoughts or instead requires a functioning brain in order to think.
Huemer reasons from the impairment of reasoning and other activities by brain injury to the conclusion that destruction of the brain at death leaves the soul unable to do anything.
Pervasive impairment from brain damage supports the conclusion that human capacities depend on the brain rather than an independently functioning soul.
The claimed systematic dependence of every human capacity on brain integrity is central evidence against a separable mental substance.
Huemer's analogy between a damaged brain and Tony Stark's damaged but replaceable Iron Man suit.
After Huemer suggests that bodily damage may merely disable a soul's equipment, Oppy appeals to the apparent vulnerability of all human capacities to brain damage.
A soul is eternal but first becomes associated with a particular body when that body first supports conscious experience.
The claim specifies how an eternal nonphysical subject relates to embodied consciousness and therefore directly develops the pro account of souls.
Asked when a soul or consciousness emerges during fetal development, Huemer distinguishes the soul's eternal existence from its becoming embodied.
If souls exist before embodiment, abortion and even refraining from conception can both deprive an existing subject of an embodied conscious life.
The argument draws a significant ethical implication from preexistence while exposing a symmetry that complicates a simple soul-based abortion argument.
Huemer argues that a subject exists before entering a fetus, then compares abortion's deprivation with the deprivation caused by declining to produce a possible child.
When an act might be extremely wrong and there is no case that it is obligatory, moral risk supplies a strong reason not to perform it.
The principle provides an independent decision-theoretic route from uncertainty about fetal personhood to caution about abortion.
Following an analogy about demolishing a possibly occupied building, Huemer formulates a general precautionary argument for avoiding potentially gravely wrongful acts.
Evidence linking relevant mental states to brain activity makes it reasonable to deny that a soul is attached to a fetus before the requisite neural activity develops.
This applies the con side's core brain-dependence case to the onset of fetal consciousness and locates it after early gestation.
Huemer's claim that an eternal soul becomes associated with a body at the first conscious experience.
Oppy answers the fetal-consciousness question by appealing to available knowledge of brain activity, while acknowledging uncertainty about the exact developmental threshold.
Infinite total future value cannot make killing harmless, because that reasoning would erase every consequentialist reason for or against any action.
The response defends the continued moral significance of embodied lives under immortal reincarnation by rejecting unrestricted infinite aggregation.
The suggestion that killing may be less serious when the victim is immortal and will be reincarnated indefinitely.
Huemer considers the thought that an immortal person's total value remains infinite regardless of death, then argues that accepting it would collapse consequentialist deliberation generally.
The infinite-value objection to consequentialism does not arise in cosmologies with a finite past, finite space, and an eventual end to life.
The qualification limits the scope of Huemer's infinity argument and shows that its force depends on substantive cosmological assumptions.
Huemer's argument that infinite total value would undermine consequentialist reasons across all choices.
Oppy responds that consequentialism survives the infinity problem in finite cosmological models, locating the difficulty specifically in an infinite universe with endless reincarnation.
The aggregate value of conscious life may be negative because most conscious beings are nonhuman animals whose lives contain severe and pervasive suffering.
The argument challenges the assumption that repeated incarnation is generally beneficial and bears directly on the value of an immortal sequence of lives.
The audience question's assumption that biologically evolved incarnations would probably have positive average value.
Huemer rejects an unexplained inference from biological evolution to positive incarnation value and emphasizes the harsh conditions faced by most nonhuman animals.
High historical infant mortality gives an independent human-centered reason to doubt that the average incarnation has positive value.
The argument reinforces doubt about beneficial reincarnation using human cases less vulnerable to uncertainty about nonhuman subjective experience.
The objection that animal lives might feel positive despite outward hardship because their subjective experience is unknown.

After the moderator questions whether animals might enjoy their distinctive experiences, Oppy points to the large historical proportion of humans dying in infancy and suggests evaluating person-years.
